response.explanation: The SQLite branch builds the ID list inline when the configured batch size is over 999. Otherwise the code uses placeholders. fetchIDs is limited by the same batch size through Limit and LimitOffset, so on SQLite the placeholder count cannot exceed 999 when the batch size is 999 or less. For deleted rows, RowsAffected equals the number of matched IDs. I saw no case where fetched IDs are non-empty but the delete affects 0 rows, other than a concurrent delete by another process. In that case the loop ends and the next scheduled run picks up the rest. A Postgres or MySQL parameter overflow would need a batch size above about 65535. I could not check the default or maximum batch size in the supplied snapshot, so I cannot show that overflow happens in normal use.

response.consequence: Every cleanup cycle writes error-level log lines with very large ID lists, even when nothing is wrong. This floods the logs, can trigger error-based alerting, and hides real errors. The batch loop also logs one more line for the final empty batch.
response.explanation: CleanAnnotations (time-based and count-based loops) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error twice per batch. One call is before the delete and one is after. They run on every batch, including successful ones with a nil error. The first call dumps the full `ids` slice, which can be up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries, plus the SQL `cond`. The `err` argument is always nil at the first call, because the error was already returned above. In the second call `err` is the delete error `y`, so even real failures are logged without being propagated differently. These look like leftover debug statements. No other code in these functions uses Debug or Info for the same data.

hypotheses.failure_mode: deleteByIDs chooses the inline-ID path based on configured batch size > 999 on SQLite, but chooses placeholders otherwise. If batch size <= 999 this is fine. However the MaxCount path with LimitOffset and the time path may return more ids than the limit in edge cases. More importantly, when RowsAffected is 0 despite ids found (e.g. rows deleted concurrently), untilDoneOrCancelled terminates early and leaves remaining rows uncleaned.
